newsitem.title: CHINA: China seen posting $6.0 bln '96 trade surplus.
newsitem.headline: China seen posting $6.0 bln '96 trade surplus.

text.p: China may post a bigger-than-expected trade surplus of around $6.0 billion in 1996 as exports recover and imports grow at a modest pace, a senior Chinese economist said on Tuesday.
"The trade surplus for all of 1996 could exceed $6.0 billion as imports are moderating," said Zhao Jinping of the Development Research Centre, a research body under the State Council or cabinet.
That would be up from recent forecasts of $4.0 billion for 1996 and a sharp improvement from estimates made early this year of trade being basically in balance.

China had a trade surplus of $8.12 billion in the first nine months of the year, aided by a solid improvement in September as exports picked up steam after a sluggish performance for most of the year. The surplus stood at $16.7 billion for all of 1995.
Export growth for most of 1996 had been stalled largely because of lengthy delays in tax rebate payments by a cash-strapped central government.
The government has since stepped up payments and that has been a key factor in the export revival, economists have said, adding that this has helped ease capital shortages across many industries.
Exports this year have also been hurt by keen competition in overseas markets, particularly in textiles and electrical goods.
Zhao told Reuters that the trade surplus could still fall back from current levels by the year-end as structural problems in the nation's trade picture remain unresolved.
Economists have long maintained that China's state industries are inefficient and in need of reform if export growth is to be sustained.
They add that most of the export gains this year have been made by foreign-invested companies, while China's state-run firms have had disappointing export records.
China's total exports are expected to grow by 1-2 percent in 1996 over last year, while overall imports could rise by 6-10 percent, Zhao said.
He said imports were rising less than expected despite a reduction in import duties starting in April, and he attributed this to the elimination of many tariff exemptions.
China trimmed duties on imports of nearly 5,000 items by an average 35.9 percent on April 1. At the same time, it scrapped tariff exemptions on imports of capital goods for foreign-funded firms.
Import growth during the first eight months of the year was 7.9 percent compared with the same period in 1995, customs figures showed. That compared with import growth of 14.2 percent in all of 1995.
